newsitem.title: USA: Boeing 737 rudder tests show no problems.
newsitem.headline: Boeing 737 rudder tests show no problems.

text.p: Aircraft maker Boeing Co said Tuesday that about two thirds of the worldwide fleet of its popular 737 aircraft have cleared a mandatory U.S. Federal Aviation Administration test for possible jamming of rudder parts with no problems found.

At the start of the month Boeing recommended that airlines using the 737, the world's most widely used jetliner with over 2,700 in service, test within 10 days for possible jamming after tests revealed the rudder's power control unit could jam when subjected to unusually harsh conditions.

While the tests were mandated by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration for all U.S.-registered 737 airplanes, Boeing said that a substantial number of 737s registered outside the U.S. have been voluntarily tested.

Operators of 737s will have to repeat the tests every 250 flight hours, or about every 30 days for the average 737. Boeing had said it is working on a modification of the jetliner that would eliminate the need for further tests.
"We're encouraged by the test results, although that doesn't mean we're not doing anything else," said Mike Denton, chief project engineer for the 737.

"We are developing an improved in-flight procedure for reacting to a jammed power control unit that will be distributed to all 737 operators. We're also continuing to assess design solutions," he added.
The 737's rudder has been a focus of investigations into the still-unexplained crashes of the Boeing aircraft in Colorado Springs in 1991 and Pittsburgh in 1994.
Boeing said that while it had discovered the potential problem with the rudder it had never been reported in more than 69 million flights by the worldwide 737 fleet.
